• Correct Answer: A (Dholavira) - Located on Khadir Bet island in the Rann of Kutch (Gujarat), Dholavira featured an advanced water management network comprising at least 16 rock-cut reservoirs, dams/bunds across the seasonal rivulets Mansar and Manhar, and stone-cut feeder channels.
• Why B is incorrect (Kalibangan): Located in Rajasthan along the dried-up Ghaggar riverbed; best known for the earliest ploughed field, fire altars, and mud-brick fortifications, not stone-built cascade reservoirs.
• Why C is incorrect (Rakhigarhi): Located in Hisar, Haryana; known as the largest Indus Valley site by area with distinct habitation mounds and cemeteries, but lacks an elaborate dam-and-reservoir water-harvesting system.
• Why D is incorrect (Ropar / Rupnagar): Located along the Sutlej in Punjab; known for yielding the first post-independence Harappan excavations and unique dog-buried-with-human grave, without large-scale water-control engineering.
• Often confused with: Lothal (Gujarat), which featured a tidal dockyard connected to the Sabarmati/Bhogavo river for maritime trade, whereas Dholavira managed freshwater harvesting through inland dams and reservoirs.
issues_found: Standard explanations often omit the names of the seasonal streams (Mansar and Manhar) harnessed at Dholavira.
Explanations frequently confuse Lothal's marine dockyard architecture with Dholavira's freshwater reservoir system.

- Pair 1 is incorrectly matched: Burzahom (Srinagar district, Jammu & Kashmir) is a prominent Neolithic-Megalithic site famous for subterranean pit-dwellings, bone tools, and unique burials (such as dogs buried with masters), not rock-cut shrines.
- Pair 2 is correctly matched: Chandraketugarh (North 24 Parganas, West Bengal) was a major river-port town famous for its elaborate Shunga-Kushana period terracotta figurines, plaques, and pottery.
- Pair 3 is correctly matched: Ganeshwar (Sikar, Rajasthan), located near the Khetri copper belt, is the type site of the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura Chalcolithic culture, renowned for hundreds of copper artefacts (arrowheads, celts, chisels, fishhooks) supplied to Harappan sites.
- Why Option A is incorrect: Pair 1 is false, and it omits valid pairs 2 and 3.
- Why Option B is incorrect: Pair 1 is false.
- Why Option C is incorrect: It omits pair 2, which is also factually correct.
- Often confused with: Burzahom's underground pit-dwellings are sometimes conflated with rock-cut chambers; pit-dwellings were cut into Karewa clay/loess soil with post-holes for timber/thatch roofs, unlike true rock-cut shrines (e.g., Barabar Caves, Ajanta) carved into solid bedrock.
issues_found: Original explanations often fail to clarify the difference between Burzahom's Neolithic pit dwellings and rock-cut cave architecture.
Explanations frequently omit the specific cultural and temporal context (e.g., Shunga-Kushana period for Chandraketugarh terracotta, Khetri link for Ganeshwar copper).
